questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the orthogonal projection of $f(t)=4{t}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by $g(t)=6t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $f(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{g(t)}$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t)=\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),g(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\cdot 6t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}24{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =[6{t}^{4}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =6-0 \\  & =6,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),g(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6t)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}36{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =[12{t}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =12-0 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t) & =\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t) \\  & =\frac{6}{12}\cdot 6t \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the orthogonal projection of $f(t)=12({t}^{2}-t)$ onto the subspace spanned by $g(t)=t-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $f(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{g(t)}$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t)=\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),g(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12{t}^{3}-24{t}^{2}+12t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[3{t}^{4}-8{t}^{3}+6{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(3-8+6)-0 \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),g(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1+1)-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t) & =\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{3})}\cdot (t-1) \\  & =3(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$ 

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2},\,g(t)=15t+3
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}$ equals $15t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=15t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(15t+3)\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}15{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{15}{4}{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{15}{4}+1)-(\frac{15}{4}-1) \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{f}_{2}(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{5}{t}^{5}|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}-(-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{2}{(\frac{2}{5})}\cdot {t}^{2}=5{t}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =15t+5{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{1}[t],$ the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most $1,$ and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1).
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=5t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=-2t+2,\,q(t)=-t-4
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{p}_{1}(t)}$ equals $-5t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t)={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)=-5t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{p}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t)=\frac{⟨q(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{p}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨q(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =q(0){p}_{2}(0)+q(1){p}_{2}(1) \\  & =(-t-4){|}_{0}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{0}+(-t-4){|}_{1}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{1} \\  & =(-4)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 0 \\  & =-8,\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={p}_{2}(0){p}_{2}(0)+{p}_{2}(1){p}_{2}(1) \\  & =(-2t+2)^{2}{|}_{0}+(-2t+2)^{2}{|}_{1} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) & =\frac{-8}{4}\cdot (-2t+2)=4t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,q(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{p}_{1}(t)}\,q(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{p}_{2}(t)}\,q(t) \\  & =-5t+(4t-4) \\  & =-t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,g(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}$ equals $5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =\frac{-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=3t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot {t}^{2}=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =3t+0 \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=2t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=6t-3$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $f(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{g(t)}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t) & =\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}2t\cdot (6t-3)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(6t-3)^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot (6t-3) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}(12{t}^{2}-6t)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{t}^{2}-36t+9)\,\text{d}t}\cdot (6t-3) \\  & =\frac{{[4{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}}{{[12{t}^{3}-18{t}^{2}+9t]}_{0}^{1}}\cdot (6t-3) \\  & =\frac{(4-3)-0}{(12-18+9)-0}\cdot (6t-3) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (6t-3) \\  & =2t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

The distance between $f(t)=2t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=6t-3$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t)‖ \\  & =‖2t-(2t-1)‖ \\  & =‖1‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨1,1⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{1}=1.$

The distance between $f(t)=5t$ and $g(t)=7t-8$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖5t-(7t-8)‖ \\  & =‖-2t+8‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨-2t+8,-2t+8⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-2t+8,-2t+8⟩ & =(-2t+8){|}_{0}\cdot (-2t+8){|}_{0}+(-2t+8){|}_{1}\cdot (-2t+8){|}_{1} \\  & =8\cdot 8+6\cdot 6 \\  & =100.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{100}=10.$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=6t$ and $g(t)=5{t}^{2}$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The distance between $f(t)=6t$ and $g(t)=5{t}^{2}$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖6t-5{t}^{2}‖ \\  & =‖5{t}^{2}-6t‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨5{t}^{2}-6t,5{t}^{2}-6t⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨5{t}^{2}-6t,5{t}^{2}-6t⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(5{t}^{2}-6t)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(25{t}^{4}-60{t}^{3}+36{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =[5{t}^{5}-15{t}^{4}+12{t}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(5-15+12)-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace
questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $2$ with real coefficients. Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

find the distance between $p(t)=7{t}^{2}-t$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t)=4{t}^{2}-4t$ with respect to the inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $p(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{q(t)}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t) & =\frac{⟨p(t),q(t)⟩}{⟨q(t),q(t)⟩}\,q(t) \\  & =\frac{p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)}{q(-1)q(-1)+q(0)q(0)+q(1)q(1)}\cdot q(t) \\  & =\frac{{\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(7{t}^{2}-t){|}_{t=i}\cdot (4{t}^{2}-4t){|}_{t=i}}{{\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(4{t}^{2}-4t){|}_{t=i}\cdot (4{t}^{2}-4t){|}_{t=i}}\cdot (4{t}^{2}-4t) \\  & =\frac{8\cdot 8+0\cdot 0+6\cdot 0}{8\cdot 8+0\cdot 0+0\cdot 0}\cdot (4{t}^{2}-4t) \\  & =\frac{64}{64}\cdot (4{t}^{2}-4t) \\  & =4{t}^{2}-4t.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The distance between $p(t)=7{t}^{2}-t$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t)=4{t}^{2}-4t$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖p(t)-{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t)‖ \\  & =‖7{t}^{2}-t-(4{t}^{2}-4t)‖ \\  & =‖3{t}^{2}+3t‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨3{t}^{2}+3t,3{t}^{2}+3t⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3{t}^{2}+3t,3{t}^{2}+3t⟩ & ={\sum }_{i\in {-1,0,1}}(3{t}^{2}+3t){|}_{t=i}\cdot (3{t}^{2}+3t){|}_{t=i} \\  & =0\cdot 0+0\cdot 0+6\cdot 6 \\  & =0+0+36 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{36}=6.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a One-Dimensional Subspace
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V = \Bbb R_1[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $1$ with real coefficients. Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
\langle p(t),q(t) \rangle = p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

find the orthogonal projection of $p(t)=-5t-3$ onto the subspace spanned by the polynomial $q(t) =t-1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $p(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{ q(t) \}$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{q(t)}\,p(t) 
= \dfrac{\langle{p(t),q(t)}\rangle}{\langle{q(t),q(t)}\rangle}\,q(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1) \\  & =(-5t-3){|}_{0}\cdot (t-1){|}_{0}+(-5t-3){|}_{1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{1} \\  & =(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-8)\cdot 0 \\  & =3+0 \\  & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

 

and

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨q(t),q(t)⟩ & =q(0)q(0)+q(1)q(1) \\  & =(t-1){|}_{0}\cdot (t-1){|}_{0}+(t-1){|}_{1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{1} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 0 \\  & =1+0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the projection is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t) & =\frac{⟨p(t),q(t)⟩}{⟨q(t),q(t)⟩}\,q(t) \\  & =\frac{3}{1}\cdot (t-1) \\  & =3(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V = \mathcal{C}[-1,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle =\int_{-1}^{1} x(t) y(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V\mathbin{:}$

$$
f_1(t)=1,\quad f_2(t)=\sin \pi t, \quad g(t)=6t^2
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{f_1(t), f_2(t)\}$ given that $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{f_1(t)\}$ equals $2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,g(t) 
= \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,g(t) + \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that $\textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,g(t) = 2,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{f_2(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
\textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t) 
= \dfrac{\langle{g(t),f_2(t)}\rangle}{\langle{f_2(t),f_2(t)}\rangle}\,f_2(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}6{t}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}6{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\sin (\pi t)$ is an odd function, while $6t^2$ is even. Hence, their product $6 t^2 \sin (\pi t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-1,1],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
\int_{-1}^{1}   6t^2 \sin (\pi t) \, \text{d}t = 0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
\textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t) = \dfrac{0}{\langle{f_2(t),f_2(t)}\rangle} \cdot  \sin \pi t = 0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =2+0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V = \Bbb R_1[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $1$ with real coefficients. Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
\langle p(t), q(t) \rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1),
$$

find the distance between $p(t) = 4t + 2$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t) = t$ with respect to the inner product.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $p(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{ q(t) \}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t) & =\frac{⟨p(t),q(t)⟩}{⟨q(t),q(t)⟩}\,q(t) \\  & =\frac{p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)}{q(0)^{2}+q(1)^{2}}\cdot q(t) \\  & =\frac{(2)(0)+(6)(1)}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot t \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

The distance between $p(t) = 4t + 2$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t) = t$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖p(t)-{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t)‖ \\  & =‖(4t+2)-6t‖ \\  & =‖-2t+2‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨-2t+2,\text{ }-2t+2⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-2t+2,\text{ }-2t+2⟩ & =(-2t+2){|}_{0}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{0}+(-2t+2){|}_{1}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{1} \\  & =(-2(0)+2)^{2}+(-2(1)+2)^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d = \sqrt{4} = 2.$
